summary: Grayson Morley's Polygon review of Marvel's Spider-Man 2 frames the game as a retelling, comparing it to Angela Carter's fairy-tale reworkings. It praises the faster traversal with web wings, the dual Peter/Miles structure, and the villains, while noting Miles's story departs more from canon than Peter's Venom arc. The review wishes the game pushed back harder against canon, as Across the Spider-Verse does, but still recommends it and looks ahead to a sequel.
one_line: Polygon's review recommends Marvel's Spider-Man 2 for its fluid traversal and dual-hero story, though it only partly breaks from Spider-Man canon.
key_facts: Marvel's Spider-Man 2 is Insomniac Games' third Spider-Man game and the first PS5-exclusive one, releasing Oct. 20 on PlayStation 5.
Players switch between Peter Parker (from Spider-Man Remastered) and Miles Morales (from his 2020 debut) at will, using the PS5's SSD for speed.

New web wings let the Spider-Men glide over rooftops and gain speed from wind tunnels without needing buildings or bridges as anchors; they are especially useful crossing the East River into the newly added Brooklyn and Queens.
The reviewer used fast travel less than in the previous two games because movement felt so fluid across the three boroughs.
Kraven the Hunter and Venom are the new principal antagonists, with large roles for returning villains the Lizard and Mister Negative.
Peter's plot retells the Venom origin story and clings most closely to canon, similar to Sam Raimi's Spider-Man 3, before pushing toward something unique to Insomniac in the late game.
Miles's story takes more liberties: Hailey Cooper returns in an MJ-esque role, and American Sign Language is featured heavily in his missions.
A Miles side quest explores Harlem's artistic history, entwining Josephine Baker, Langston Hughes, and Charlie Parker with the fictional history of SHIELD.
The opening sequence has Sandman coating the city in dust as Peter and Miles help first responders, with eerie echoes of 9/11.
The review compares the game to Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse, whose villain Spider-Man 2099 enforces 'canon events' that Miles resists.
Themes such as mass incarceration, recidivism, and the surveillance state appear fleetingly but are not developed due to the constant set-pieces.
The reviewer laments the 'Frankenstein-ification' of the boroughs ('RIP Chelsea') and says the sequel is teed up for the Bronx.
The game was reviewed using a pre-release download code provided by Sony Interactive Entertainment.
